The flour is dry: "The flour is dry" refers to the state of flour when it has not absorbed any moisture or liquid. In this condition, the flour remains in its loose, powdery form, without any clumps or dampness. If any moisture like water or egg is added, it is no longer dry.
The flour is mixed with water: "The flour is mixed with water" refers to the state of flour that has been combined with water. If it is sufficiently kneaded or cooked so that it lose the fluidity, "The flour is mixed with water" is no longer applicable.
The flour is combined with other ingredi: "The flour is combined with other ingredients" refers to the state of flour that has been combined with other components in a recipe. It doesn't refer to adding only seasonings or water.
The flour is lumpy: "The flour is lumpy" refers to the state of flour when it contains small clumps or aggregates, often as a result of moisture exposure or poor storage conditions. If the flour is sufficiently kneaded to remove the clumps, "The flour is lumpy" is no longer applicable.
The flour is kneaded (dough): "The flour is kneaded dough" refers to the state of flour that has been mixed with water and worked together by hand or with a machine until it forms a cohesive and elastic mass. Once the dough is flattened or cooked, "The flour is kneaded dough" is no longer applicable.
The flour is flattened: "The flour is flattened" refers to the state of flour when it has been kneaded and spread out or pressed down to create a thin, even layer. If it is not flattened, "The flour is flattened" is not applicable.
The flour is baked: "The flour is baked" refers to the state of flour that has undergone a cooking process, typically in an oven or another heat source, which transforms its raw form into a firmer, cohesive and often golden-brown structure.
The flour is fried: "The flour is fried" refers to the state of flour that has been cooked in panful of oil until it changes into crispy texture and often golden-brown color.
